## The method is never the whole story

On Monday, we used disciplines to see different parts of a management problem.

<br>

Today we ask the prior question: **What assumptions lead a team to call one kind
of evidence persuasive, relevant, or sufficient?**

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3. Use a familiar contrast: a survey can
show a broad pattern; it cannot, on its own, show how every community makes
meaning of that pattern. Neither fact makes one method universally superior.
:::

## By the end of class, you can

- distinguish ontology, epistemology, methodology, and axiology;
- compare how paradigms shape questions and evidence; and
- select a defensible combination of approaches for a contested decision.

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3--7.3.3. These objectives prepare
students to identify assumptions and then use them in a management case.
:::

## A paradigm is a working worldview {.section-slide .divider-plan background-color="#123f5a"}

<br>

It shapes what a researcher takes to be real, how knowledge can be developed,
which methods fit, and what purposes should guide inquiry.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. Make the term less intimidating:
students already make assumptions when they decide that a number, story, map, or
meeting should carry weight in a decision.
:::

## Can one discipline use different paradigms?

**Yes.** A discipline is a field of inquiry; a paradigm is a set of assumptions
that guides inquiry.

<br>

Two sociologists studying mountain lion management might ask:

- How do community norms relate to support for a proposed action?
- What meanings do residents attach to mountain lions?

<br>

Both work within sociology. They may begin from different paradigms.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2.1.2, 7.3.1--7.3.2; mountain lion example adapted for
class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.2.1.2, 7.3.1--7.3.2. Connect Monday's
disciplinary lens to today's philosophical lens. The first question seeks a
pattern; the second seeks meaning. Both belong within sociology, so a discipline
does not prescribe one paradigm. This example illustrates the distinction rather
than assigning a paradigm solely from a question or method. Do not name the five
paradigms yet; they are introduced later in the deck.
:::

## Four questions sit underneath a research design {.smaller}

<br>

  | Foundation | Plain-language question |
  | --- | --- |
  | **Ontology** | What is real here? |
  | **Epistemology** | What can we know, and how? |
  | **Methodology** | What process can produce credible knowledge? |
  | **Axiology** | What values and responsibilities guide the inquiry? |

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 5 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Give a deer-management example. One
team may treat attitude as a measurable construct; another may focus on the
different meanings residents attach to deer. Both must still explain how their
approach produces credible knowledge and how it will be used.
:::

## Good research names its values and responsibilities

<br>

Researchers and managers make choices about:

- which problems are worth studying;
- whose experiences and knowledge are included;
- what harms to avoid; and
- how findings should be used.

<br>

Naming those choices makes research responsibilities more visible.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.1. Connect to Weeks 4--5: a monitoring
system is built around objectives, and governance determines who helps set them.
Axiology is not an excuse to ignore evidence; it clarifies what evidence is
being sought and why.
:::

## The same mountain lion issue can generate different rigorous questions

<br>

  | Starting point    | A question it makes possible                          |
  | ---               | ---                                                   |
  | Measure a pattern | What share of residents supports a proposed action?   |
  | Interpret meaning | What do mountain lions mean to different communities? |
  | Examine power     | Whose voices are missing from management decisions?   |
  | Solve a problem   | What evidence mix supports a workable decision?       |

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2. These are adapted from the chapter's
key point. Ask students which question a statewide survey answers best and which
require a different design. Do not characterize any one question as the
"correct" starting point in all contexts.
:::

## 5 major research traditions relevant to HD

<br>

  | Paradigm                       | Starting point                                                         |
  | ------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | Positivism                     | Measure a reality that exists independently.                           |
  | Post-positivism                | Measure carefully while accounting for uncertainty.                    |
  | Interpretivism                 | Understand the meanings people make.                                   |
  | Critical paradigm              | Examine how power shapes knowledge and decisions.                      |
  | Pragmatism                     | Use approaches that fit the decision at hand.                          |

<br> They are **not the only paradigms**, and researchers still use them.
Together they show how assumptions about measurement, uncertainty, meaning,
power, and action shape research questions and evidence.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1--7.3.2.5.
:::

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1--7.3.2.5. This is the students'
first introduction to the five named paradigms; the next slide begins with
positivism. The chapter calls these major paradigms relevant to human
dimensions, not an exhaustive list. Its reason for teaching paradigms is that
they shape questions, credible evidence, and interpretation. The five also give
students a useful contrast among measurement, uncertainty, meaning, power, and
practical action; that teaching rationale is an inference from the chapter's
sequence. They remain in use, though researchers do not have to belong to only
one or use a label in exactly the same way. Do not ask students to classify the
mountain lion questions before teaching each paradigm. Indigenous ways of
knowing follow later as complete knowledge systems, not a sixth technique in
this table.
:::

## Positivism: measure a reality that exists independently

**Where we start:** the most measurement-focused tradition. Each paradigm that
follows keeps or questions part of this view.

<br>

Reality exists independently of what people believe about it. Careful
observation and experiments can reveal measurable patterns and effects.

<br>

A researcher could test whether a specific message changes support for a
proposed mountain lion action.

<br>

**Therefore:** define the outcome, compare responses systematically, and measure
the effect.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.1. The chapter tests whether a
habitat-restoration message changes support; this slide adapts the question to
mountain lion management. Explain why an experiment and clear measures fit a
bounded causal question. Meanings, histories, and unequal power may remain
outside what this measurement can answer. The top line sets up the sequence:
each later slide opens by naming what it keeps from, or breaks with, the one
before. That sequence is a teaching device; the chapter lists the paradigms in
this order but only calls post-positivism an evolution of positivism.
:::

## Post-positivism: measure carefully and stay revisable

**From positivism:** keeps the belief that reality exists and the commitment to
systematic evidence. Questions whether we can ever measure it exactly.

<br>

We can only approximate reality. Uncertainty, bias, and error shape every
observation, so conclusions stay open to revision.

<br>

A survey can estimate support for a mountain lion action, but who responds and
how the question is asked can affect the estimate.

<br>

**Therefore:** report uncertainty, check bias and alternative explanations, and
revise conclusions when new evidence arrives.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.2. Contrast with the prior slide:
post-positivism retains systematic inquiry but treats a finding as an
approximation, not a final reading of reality. The chapter's example is a survey
about chronic-wasting-disease management; the slide adapts that logic to the
mountain lion issue. Ask what could change the survey estimate: who was sampled,
who responded, question wording, or a plausible alternative explanation.
Post-positivism is not limited to surveys or quantitative methods; the chapter
allows qualitative and mixed methods when inquiry is systematic, transparent,
and open to revision.
:::

## Interpretivism: examine how people make meaning

**From post-positivism:** a sharper break. There is no single reality to
approximate; the same issue can hold multiple realities for different people.

<br>

People make meaning through experience, culture, and context. The same wildlife
issue can mean different things to different people.

<br>

A researcher could ask residents what mountain lions and their management mean
to them.

<br>

**Therefore:** gather open-ended accounts and interpret differences in context
rather than force them into one average.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. The top line reflects the
chapter's contrast: the goal is not one single reality but the multiple
realities people experience. Contrast the question with the prior measurement
examples: the goal is to understand meanings in context, not estimate one
population average. The mountain lion example adapts the chapter's
wolf-reintroduction example. The next slide explains how open-ended inquiry can
still be systematic.
:::

## Interpretive evidence is systematic, not "just stories"

Interviews, focus groups, participant observation, and narrative analysis can be
designed carefully to examine how people construct meaning.

<br>

For mountain lion management, an interpretive study might ask how ranchers,
Tribal members, agency staff, and urban residents each describe mountain lions
and their management.

<br>

The goal is to understand context and differences in meaning---not to force them
into a single account.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.3. Connect to the Arizona and
commercial-fisher examples from Week 4: qualitative evidence can identify a
blind spot in a measurement system. Rigor comes from transparent design and
interpretation, not from pretending a lived experience is a percentage.
:::

## Critical paradigm: examine how power shapes knowledge

**From interpretivism:** keeps the idea that reality is socially constructed.
Adds that power and privilege shape whose construction counts.

<br>

History and power shape whose knowledge is heard and who bears the consequences
of a decision.

<br>

A researcher could ask whose concerns shaped a mountain lion management proposal
and whose concerns were left out.

<br>

**Therefore:** examine exclusion and inequity, and ask whether the research
reinforces or challenges them.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.4. Connect directly to Week 5: a
participation process can appear inclusive while still withholding influence.
The mountain lion question adapts the chapter's examples of historical exclusion
and whose knowledge is treated as legitimate. Ask what evidence would reveal
exclusion and what a team would owe people once it recognized it. The paradigm
carries an explicit commitment to justice and social change. Link to the prior
paradigm: the chapter says the critical paradigm views reality as socially
constructed, like interpretivism, but emphasizes power and privilege.
:::

## Pragmatism: choose evidence that serves the decision

**From the other four:** does not start from one objective truth or one
constructed reality. It asks which knowledge is useful for this problem.

<br>

Knowledge is a tool for solving problems. The question, context, and constraints
guide the choice of methods.

<br>

For a mountain lion decision, a team could combine a survey of support with
interviews about reasons and meetings to test options.

<br>

**Therefore:** choose a credible evidence mix that fits the decision, budget,
and timeline.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5; mountain lion example adapted for class.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.2.5. The chapter's example combines
surveys, interviews, and meetings to study angler satisfaction; this slide
adapts that logic to a hypothetical mountain lion decision. Avoid describing
pragmatism as "anything goes." Each approach still needs a defensible fit with
the question, evidence, feasibility, transparency, and decision process. Link to
the prior paradigms: the chapter says pragmatism does not focus primarily on one
objective truth or one constructed reality, and often combines multiple
approaches and methods.
:::

## Indigenous knowledge systems are not an add-on data source {.section-slide .divider-learn background-color="#123f5a"}

**From the five paradigms:** those are Western traditions. Indigenous knowledge
systems answer the same four questions from their own foundations.

<br> They are complete, place-based systems of knowledge, practice,
relationship, responsibility, and governance.

::: notes
Time: 1 minute. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3. The top line follows the chapter's
own transition: the paradigms above are Western academic traditions, and
Indigenous worldviews possess their own ontology, epistemology, methodology, and
axiology. Point back to the four-questions slide. This is not a sixth paradigm
on the list. State this plainly before any example. Do not collapse distinct
Nations, communities, or knowledge systems into one generic category.
:::

## Two-Eyed Seeing: work from the strengths of both eyes

<br>

**Etuaptmumk**, often translated as *Two-Eyed Seeing*, is a Mi'kmaw concept that
recognizes the value of Indigenous and Western knowledge systems while seeking
respectful, meaningful partnership.

<br>

It is not a shortcut for extracting local observations into a Western project.
It requires attention to relationships, sovereignty, and who guides the work.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1.
:::

::: notes
Time: 4 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §7.3.3.1. Pair this with the governance
lecture: Tribal governments are sovereign decision-makers, not simply a
stakeholder group. Emphasize that the concept names an orientation toward
respectful partnership, not a universal method that others can claim without
relationship or accountability.
:::

## Case diagnosis: choose evidence without choosing sides

<br>

**Scenario:** A state agency must revise a drought-season fishing closure. It
has creel data, temperature records, and public comments, but hears that its
current process misses subsistence and Tribal fishing perspectives.

In groups of three:

1. Name one question the agency must answer.
2. Name two kinds of evidence or knowledge that fit it.
3. State one process condition required for that evidence to be used
   responsibly.

::: notes
Time: 8 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3--7.3.3. Debrief toward fit and
accountability. Good answers may include biological thresholds plus community
experience, but require a process that recognizes sovereignty and does not ask
one group to validate a decision already made.
:::

## Friday

<br>

Read the **Week 06 Case Brief: Four Proposals on One Desk --- The Thornapple
Lake Decision** before class. All case facts are in it; bring the concepts from
Chapter 7 and this week's class work.

<br>

Four rigorous proposals, one $180,000 budget, an eight-month deadline, and a
late letter from a Tribal fisheries program setting a condition about who owns
the knowledge.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1--7.3.3.
:::

::: notes
Time: 3 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3.1--7.3.3. Tell students the roles this
week are question and paradigm lead, methods and evidence lead, and standpoint
and limits lead, and that the group and role roster is already published. Warn
them that the budget arithmetic is part of the grade: Proposal 4 alone leaves
$30,000, and Proposal 3 runs a month past the deadline. For combinations, costs
add but the components run concurrently, so the longest component determines the
timeline.
:::

## Close: rigor is a match among question, evidence, and responsibility

Paradigms make our assumptions inspectable. That is useful because management
decisions need evidence that is credible **and** a process that is appropriate
to the people, places, and consequences involved.

**Next week:** use psychology to move from "people should care more" to a
specific, observable behavior and a plausible strategy.

::: {.source-note}
Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3--7.4.
:::

::: notes
Time: 2 minutes. Source: Chapter 7, §§7.3--7.4. Exit prompt: What assumption
about evidence do you now notice in a management claim? Use a few responses to
open the next class, then connect to Chapter 8's behavior frameworks.
:::
